sentences.text: Shingopana is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod whose name means "wide neck" in Swahili.
This quadrupedal sauropod grew up to 8 meters long, making it smaller than the average sauropod.
The holotype fossil shows evidence of insect bore holes that damaged the remains shortly after the animal died.
Remnants of a bulbous expansion on the cervical vertebrae likely helped to strengthen Shingopana's neck.
Part of the holotype skeleton was discovered in 2002 by scientists from the Rukwa Rift Basin Project led by Patrick O'Connor and Nancy Stevens.
The species Shingopana songwensis was officially named in 2017.
Four incomplete ribs with flanged edges were found in the holotype, though their specific function remains unknown.
Shingopana belongs to the unranked family Titanosauria.
The parent group for Shingopana is Lithostrotia.
Phylogenetic testing suggests Shingopana is more closely related to the South American Aeolosaurini family than to any African titanosaurs found to date.
Shingopana fossils were found in the Upper Cretaceous Galula Formation within the Rukwa Rift Basin in Tanzania.
The time range for Shingopana is estimated from the Cenomanian to the Campanian, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.
Shingopana coexisted with other sauropods like Rukwatitan and Mnyamawamtuka, various crocodiles, the mammal Galulatherium, and lungfish in its ecosystem.
